opus-5.5.text:
That's a good question. When I was a student, a lot of what I did came from curiosity and some naivety. With XGBoost, or later the early days of TVM, I didn't fully know how hard things would be. If I had known how much engineering, maintenance, and community building it would take, I might have hesitated. In a way, not knowing gave me the courage to just start.

Now that I have more experience, I understand the cost of a project much better. I know a system isn't just the first prototype. It's the years of iteration, the users who depend on it, and the people you work with. So I've become more deliberate. I ask whether the problem really matters, whether it fits a bigger direction I believe in, and whether I'm the right person, with the right group, to do it.

But I don't think experience should make you less willing to take risks. It should make you take better risks. Experience helps you see which parts are truly hard and which only look scary. Then you can be bolder about the important, uncertain parts, because you're more confident handling the rest.

I also try to keep some of that student mindset. I still like to build a small prototype first and see whether the idea has life. Often the best projects begin as something you're curious about, and only later do you realize it could be bigger. So I'd say experience changed how I choose and plan projects, but I hope it hasn't taken away the joy of jumping into something new.

r001.rationale: He says experience has made him more deliberate about a project’s importance, fit, and whether he and the group are suited to it, but does not say he is more inclined to question whether the project can succeed.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and I think the honest answer is that it's changed in two opposite directions at once.

On one hand, experience makes you more cautious, because you've seen how many projects fail. When I was a student working on early machine learning systems, I would just dive in. I didn't know how hard distributed training was, or how much engineering goes into making something like a gradient boosting library actually robust. That ignorance was almost useful. If I had fully understood the scope of XGBoost or TVM at the start, I might have hesitated. So in that sense, experience gives you a better sense of cost, and that can make you say no more often.

On the other hand, experience makes you much more willing to take on things that look impossible, because you've learned that the hard part is usually not the idea. It's the sustained effort, the community, the iteration. Once you've gone through that cycle a few times, you know what the valley of despair looks like in the middle of a project, and you know it's survivable. That gives you a kind of confidence that a first-time builder doesn't have.

So now I'd say I'm pickier about which projects to start, but once I commit, I'm much more stubborn about seeing them through. I also think more about whether a project can become a foundation for other people. The question I ask now isn't just "can I build this?" but "if this works, does it enable a hundred other things?" That's the filter experience has given me.

r001.rationale: He says experience makes him more cautious because he has seen projects fail, and that he now asks whether he can build a project—conveying greater scrutiny of whether a project can succeed.

astra-6.text:
I think experience can actually make you more hesitant to pursue a project, because you see more of the things that could go wrong. When you’re starting out, you might just think, “This sounds interesting. Let’s try it.” Later, you can come up with ten reasons why it might not work before you even begin.

So I try to use experience to figure out how to approach a problem, without letting it decide too early that the problem isn’t worth pursuing. You don’t need to know that the whole project will succeed. Sometimes you just need an interesting question and a small first step that lets you learn something.

r001.rationale: The response says experience can make him more hesitant because he sees more ways a project could go wrong and can list reasons it might not work.

sol-6.1.text: I think experience cuts both ways. When you’re starting out, you don’t know all the reasons something might not work, so you’re willing to try. As you gain experience, you can recognize the difficulties earlier, and that can make you more cautious. But you also gain confidence that you can work through some of those difficulties. So I try to use experience to figure out where to start and what to test first, while keeping that willingness to explore something I don’t fully understand yet.

r001.rationale: The response says experience can reveal difficulties earlier and make someone more cautious, but it does not clearly say Tianqi is more inclined to question whether a project can succeed.
